summary: The Mohr's circle calculator turns the principal stress and the maximum shear stress into mean stress (σₘ). It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Mohr's circle calculator work?
sections.html:
The Mohr's circle calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports mean stress (σₘ) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the principal stress (σ₁), the principal stress (σ₂) and the maximum shear stress (τₘₐₓ).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Mohr's circle calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Mean stress (σₘ)=(1 ÷ 2) × normal stress in the X direction (σₓₓ) + (1 ÷ 2) × normal stress in the Y direction (σyy)
Normal stress in the X direction (σₓₓ)=((principal stress (σ₁) ^ 2) − principal stress (σ₁) × normal stress in the Y direction (σyy) − (shear stress (τₓy) ^ 2)) ÷ (principal stress (σ₁) − normal stress in the Y direction (σyy))
Normal stress in the X direction (σₓₓ)=((principal stress (σ₂) ^ 2) − principal stress (σ₂) × normal stress in the Y direction (σyy) − (shear stress (τₓy) ^ 2)) ÷ (principal stress (σ₂) − normal stress in the Y direction (σyy))
Normal stress in the X direction (σₓₓ)=normal stress in the Y direction (σyy) + 2 × the square root of ((maximum shear stress (τₘₐₓ) ^ 2) − (shear stress (τₓy) ^ 2))
Von Mises stress (σMiₛₑₛ)=the square root of ((normal stress in the X direction (σₓₓ) ^ 2) − normal stress in the X direction (σₓₓ) × normal stress in the Y direction (σyy) + (normal stress in the Y direction (σyy) ^ 2) + 3 × (shear stress (τₓy) ^ 2))
Shear stress (τyₓ)=-shear stress (τₓy)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Normal stress in the X direction (σₓₓ) = 10 MPa and Normal stress in the Y direction (σyy) = 10 MPa. Working through the relationship above gives Mean stress (σₘ) = 10 MPa.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Mean stress (σₘ) = 10 MPa should be roughly the size you expected from Normal stress in the X direction (σₓₓ) = 10 MPa and Normal stress in the Y direction (σyy) = 10 MPa.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Mohr's circle calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the principal stress and the maximum shear stress — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Mohr's circle calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns mean stress (σₘ), derived from the principal stress and the maximum shear stress. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Mohr's circle calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the principal stress and the maximum shear stress, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter normal stress in the X direction (σₓₓ) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Normal stress in the X direction (σₓₓ) opens in megapascals and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Mean stress (σₘ) = 10 MPa. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Mohr's circle calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
